packet: Boundary conversion, boundary production, and individuation
scope: Primary passages for three distinct accounts of how systems and their surroundings relate. No historical influence between Beer, Simondon, and autopoiesis is inferred.

sources.title: The Position of the Problem of Ontogenesis
sources.locator: Printed pp. 9–12, especially p. 11, definition of transduction and crystallisation example; p. 12, distinction from deduction and induction
sources.verified: Publisher-hosted translation inspected. Printed p. 11 is PDF page 8. The definition and example are in Simondon's text, not the translator's explanatory notes.
sources.limits: 2009 dates this translation, not the origin of Simondon's theory. Intermittent publisher timeouts occurred after successful reading. No priority or influence claim is made. Link and paraphrase only.

sources.locator: Sections 2–4, pp. 187–189; section 7, pp. 191–192; section 9, pp. 192–193

sources.title: The Organization of the Living: A Theory of the Living Organization
sources.publisher: Original: International Journal of Man-Machine Studies 7(3), pp. 313–332; inspected reprint: International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 51 (1999), pp. 149–168
sources.locator: Inspected 1999 reprint: 'Preliminary concepts', pp. 151–152; 'Implicit requirements' and 'Plasticity and structural coupling', pp. 155–156; 'Descriptive fallacy', pp. 157–158; 'Structural coupling', pp. 162–163

nodes.label: Transduction in Simondon
nodes.summary: Simondon's account of individuation through progressive structuring: each formed region helps constitute the next. It differs from converting signals across an organisational boundary.

nodes.label: Gilbert Simondon
nodes.summary: Author of the account of individuation and transduction presented here through Gregory Flanders's 2009 translation of his introduction.

nodes.label: Autopoiesis
nodes.summary: A network produces components that regenerate that network and constitute it as a distinguishable unity. The 1974 paper makes this a specific organisational condition, not a synonym for persistence.

profiles.canonical_definition: Progressive structuring through which an individual takes form; constituted structure enables further structuring.
profiles.summary: Crystallisation is Simondon's simplest example. His question concerns the coming-into-being of individuals and relations, rather than starting with two already constituted domains.
profiles.why_it_matters: Readers can ask whether an intervention changes a connection between established parties or changes what the parties become. This practical question is an editorial comparison.
key_distinctions: A philosophical account versus a demonstrated organisational mechanism
practice_connections: Name which meaning of transduction an argument requires.
common_misreadings: The shared word establishes a shared theory or historical influence.
open_checks: Applications require their own evidence; this route does not establish a Beer–Simondon lineage.

locators.claim: Definition, crystallisation example, and the status of terms arising through transduction.

profiles.canonical_definition: Self-production of a unity through a recursively constituted network of component production.
profiles.summary: The biological account includes the production of a boundary that enables the processes producing it. Material turnover is compatible with the persistence of this organisation.
profiles.why_it_matters: A boundary drawn by an analyst and a boundary produced by a living system make different claims.
practice_connections: Before applying the term, identify components, production processes, and boundary formation.
common_misreadings: Any durable feedback loop is autopoietic.
Calling an institution living establishes biological autopoiesis.
open_checks: Social applications need an explicit account of what is being produced.

locators.locator: Section 3, p. 188; section 7, pp. 191–192; section 9, pp. 192–193
locators.claim: Definition, boundary-production condition, and identification criteria.
The living unity depends on a medium and exchanges elements with it.

profiles.canonical_definition: Varela, Maturana, and Uribe's 1974 paper specifying autopoietic organisation and illustrating it with a tessellation model.
profiles.summary: The paper specifies a self-producing organisation, illustrates it with a tessellation model, and gives six criteria for identifying an autopoietic unity. Its boundary must arise through the system's own processes.
profiles.why_it_matters: The paper makes the claim inspectable against explicit conditions.
key_distinctions: An illustrative model versus empirical confirmation
practice_connections: Use section 9 to examine a proposed application.
common_misreadings: Publication in a foundational collection settles every later application.
open_checks: Independent reproduction of the model remains outside this review.

profiles.canonical_definition: Repeated interactions through which systems and their environments shape the structures governing later interactions. In Maturana's biological account, these structural changes conserve the system's defining organisation.
profiles.summary: Maturana distinguishes a perturbation that triggers change from an instruction that specifies it: the current structure determines the response. Fractal Enterprise Model practice uses structural coupling to examine consequential enterprise–environment relationships; that application requires its own account of the participating systems and interactions.
profiles.why_it_matters: A repeated message can meet a changing recipient. Communication problems may involve the history of the relationship as well as the message.
practice_connections: Trace how repeated interactions alter the parties' capacity to respond; treat this as an interpretive question, not a biological diagnosis.
common_misreadings: An external message determines the recipient's response.
open_checks: Evidence is needed for any proposed organisational application.

locators.locator: 1999 reprint, 'Plasticity and structural coupling', pp. 155–156; 'Descriptive fallacy', pp. 157–158; 'Structural coupling', pp. 162–163
locators.claim: History, structural determination, and the distinction from semantic instruction.

edges.label: is formulated in this account by
edges.locator: Printed p. 11; author and translator identified on p. 4
edges.scope: Simondon formulates transduction as progressive structuring through which individuation occurs. This attributes the inspected account without claiming that he originated the word.

edges.label: concerns individuation rather than the boundary conversion described by
edges.locator: Simondon, printed pp. 11–12; Beer, 2002 electronic edition of the 1989 text, PDF pp. 6–8 and Appendix 2, p. 16, third principle
edges.scope: Simondon examines individuation through progressive structuring; Beer examines conversion at organisational boundaries and the variety a transducer must handle. This editorial comparison distinguishes the questions addressed without inferring direct influence or equivalence.

edges.label: defines and models
edges.scope: The paper defines autopoiesis through a network of component production and illustrates that organisation in a tessellation model. The illustration does not itself establish later biological or social applications.

edges.label: requires an autopoietic unity to produce its
edges.scope: The paper requires an autopoietic unity's boundary to be generated by its component interactions and sustained by the processes it enables. An analyst's selected boundary alone does not meet that condition.

edges.label: grounds the biological sense of
edges.scope: Varela, Maturana, and Uribe explain biological autonomy through the continued production of the organisation constituting the unity. This sense of autonomy differs from managerial discretion or political independence.

edges.label: adds a question about the changing recipient to
edges.locator: Maturana, 1999 reprint, pp. 162–163; Beer, 2002 electronic edition of the 1989 text, PDF pp. 6–8 and Appendix 2, p. 16, third principle
edges.scope: Maturana's account asks how interactions alter the structures determining future responses; Beer's account asks how a boundary transducer handles the distinctions carried by a channel. Comparing them raises a practical question about changes in the recipient as well as the message, without equating the concepts.

reader_route.title: What happens at a boundary?
reader_route.question: Does the account concern a message changing form, parties changing through interaction, a unity producing its boundary, or an individual taking form?
reader_route.editorial_note: Use the same practical situation to ask different questions. Do not use the sequence as a genealogy, or merge the meanings because their vocabulary overlaps.
